draft.title: Sources of law
card: Law comes from two main sources. One is parliament. The other is the decisions judges make in court cases.
law made by parliament. It is written down in an Act of Parliament, such as the Crimes Act 1958 (Vic).
law made by judges when they decide cases. It is also called case law, and it is recorded in the written reasons for a decision.
Parliament is elected by the people. Judges are not elected. If a statute and the common law disagree on the same matter, parliament can change the law by passing a new Act.
draft.remember: Statute law comes from parliament's Acts. Common law comes from judges' decisions.

a.q: Which of these is an example of common law?
opts: A rule set out in a judge's reasons for deciding a case
A rule set out in a new Act passed by parliament
A rule set out in a bill before parliament
A rule set out in a council's list of local fees
a.why: Common law is made by judges when they decide cases, and it is recorded in their reasons. An Act of Parliament is statute law, not common law. A bill is only a proposed law until parliament passes it.

b.q: Parliament passes an Act that changes a rule judges had set in earlier cases. Which statement is correct?
opts: The new rule is statute law and replaces the judges' rule
The new rule is common law because it replaces a case
The judges' rule stays in force over the new Act
The new rule is common law until a court approves it
b.why: An Act of Parliament is statute law, whatever the topic. Parliament can change the law by passing a new Act, so the Act replaces the judges' rule. Where a case once set the rule, that does not make a later Act common law.
b.clue: Look at who made the new rule, not what it replaced.

a.best: A rule set out in a judge's reasons for deciding a case

b.best: The new rule is statute law and replaces the judges' rule

problems.detail: 'If a statute and the common law disagree on the same matter, parliament can change the law by passing a new Act' is muddled. Where a statute and the common law conflict, the statute already prevails, and no new Act is needed. The card never states plainly that statute law overrides inconsistent common law, yet question b relies on that idea.

The lines on parliament being elected, judges not being elected, and parliament overriding judge-made law explain how parliament and the courts relate. That belongs to point 4 (Parliament and the courts) rather than to sources of law.

check.summary: Both answers are clear and correct. The card's last line is muddled: it suggests a new Act is needed when statute and common law conflict, instead of saying statute prevails. That parliament-and-courts material also belongs to point 4.

proposal.title: Sources of law
card: Law in Victoria comes from two main sources: parliament, and the decisions judges make when they decide court cases.
law made by parliament and set out in an Act of Parliament, such as the Crimes Act 1958 (Vic). A bill is only a proposed law until parliament passes it.
law made by judges when they decide cases. It is also called case law, and it is recorded in the judge's written reasons for the decision.
The two sources do not rank equally. Where a statute and a common law rule are inconsistent, the statute prevails and the common law rule no longer applies.
proposal.remember: Acts make statute law, judges' decisions make common law, and statute wins if they clash.
